# Installing the heron service

Run `make bootstrap` once on a new machine. It installs the pinned toolchain and creates the local configuration in `config/local.toml`.

## Requirements

The service needs PostgreSQL 16 and Redis 7. Older PostgreSQL releases are not supported because the migrations use generated columns.

## First start

Start the stack with `make up`. The web console listens on port 8420 and the API on port 8421.

# Release checklist

Releases are cut from the `main` branch every second Thursday.

## Before tagging

Update the changelog, run the full integration suite and ask the on-call engineer to approve the release ticket.

## Rollback

If error rates double within an hour of a deploy, roll back with `make rollback VERSION=<previous>` and open an incident.

# Decision: object storage

We store uploaded attachments in an S3-compatible bucket rather than on the database server. The bucket is called `heron-uploads` and objects expire after 400 days.

Large files over 2 GB are rejected at the upload endpoint because the proxy times out on longer transfers.

# Decision: sign-in

Staff sign in through the company single sign-on provider. Local passwords were removed in version 3.2.

Service accounts use short-lived tokens that are rotated every twelve hours by the token broker.

On-call rotation

The on-call engineer changes every Monday at 10:00. Pages go to the #heron-oncall channel first and escalate to the team lead after fifteen minutes without acknowledgement.

The current escalation contact for database incidents is the platform team.

# Retired plan: mobile client

We once planned a native tablet client called Kestrel with offline sync. The project was cancelled after the prototype review.
